10.1002_adfm.79407: Developing passivators that deliver multi‐mechanistic synergistic effects constitutes a highly efficacious strategy for crystallization regulation, while simultaneously serving as a critical approach to bolster the long‐term operational stability of perovskite solar cells. In this work, a series of amine‐derived functional additives was rationally engineered and systematically evaluated via molecular design strategy to precisely regulate both the substitution pattern and the chlorine atoms count. Notably, the dichloro‐substituted derivative 1‐(3,4‐dichlorophenyl)‐3‐(pyridin‐4‐yl)urea (DCLPU) demonstrates exceptional coordination passivation capability, an effect predominantly ascribed to the significantly enhanced electronegativity of its carbonyl group. This modification markedly reduces the perovskite crystallization rate and directs the preferential orientation of the perovskite (100) crystal facet. Furthermore, DCLPU suppresses non‑radiative recombination losses and weakens electron‑phonon coupling via energy level modulation. Consequently, the inverted device incorporating DCLPU attained a champion power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 27.32% (certified: 26.91%), alongside a corresponding module efficiency of 22.50%. These devices further exhibited outstanding thermal stability, ultraviolet resistance, and sustained operational durability. This work delineates a robust and practicable paradigm for advancing high‐efficiency, stable perovskite photovoltaic technologies.
10.1002_adma.202508315: Eutectic electrolytes (EEs) are promising for zinc‐metal batteries. However, traditional EEs suffer from high viscosity and severe ion migration hysteresis. Although hydration improves ion transport, it simultaneously intensifies corrosion‐related issues. Here, an original electrolyte system based on a double eutectic electrolyte (DEE) is proposed that employs strong Lewis acid‐base interactions in the inner solvation shell alongside a reconstructed hydrogen‐bonding network in the outer solvation shell, thereby achieving a good balance between ion transport kinetics and corrosion challenges. Moreover, the DEE modulates the electrochemical interface to form a stable and effective solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer, mitigating water corrosion and promoting uniform Zn deposition. Thus, symmetric cells based on the DEE demonstrate significantly extended cycle lives of 5900 h at 1 mA cm −2 , 1 mAh cm −2 with minimal voltage polarization, and maintain over 3300 h even at 4 mA cm −2 , 4 mAh cm −2 . The system also demonstrates outstanding performance at −20 °C, sustaining long‐term cycling up to 8000 h at 0.5 mA cm −2 . Furthermore, full cells with a low N/P ratio of 5.89 achieve stable cycling for 1000 cycles with 82.4% capacity retention, and pouch cells (mass loading: 103 mg) exhibit excellent durability over 2000 cycles at 0.5 A g −1 .
10.1002_aenm.71680: The rapid growth of lithium‐ion batteries is intensifying pressure on critical‐material supply chains while generating increasing volumes of complex battery waste. However, existing recycling technologies struggle to process mixed feedstocks efficiently and often recover products with limited added value. Here, we advance beyond cathode‐focused hydrometallurgical recycling by integrating composition‐adjustable cathode resynthesis with the purification and surface modification of co‐recovered graphite, followed by full‐pouch‐cell validation and unified process‐level assessment. Mixed low‐nickel cathodes are upgraded to high‐performance LiNi 0.6 Mn 0.2 Co 0.2 O 2 (NMC622) with improved lithium‐ion transport and cycling stability. Meanwhile, a closed‐loop graphite upcycling process produces battery‐grade anodes with enhanced interfacial kinetics and durability. Full pouch cells assembled entirely from the upcycled materials exhibit fewer side reactions and approximately twice the cycle life of cells using commercial counterparts, retaining 70% of their capacity after 2590 cycles. Techno‐economic and life‐cycle analyses further indicate >95% recycled‐material utilization, 22.9% higher profitability, and reductions of 27.0% in greenhouse‐gas emissions and 29.4% in energy consumption relative to the reference recycling route. These findings establish mixed battery waste as a viable feedstock for producing high‐value battery materials and demonstrate a pathway from conventional resource recovery toward value‐added remanufacturing for circular, resilient, and low‐carbon battery supply chains.
10.1016_j.electacta.2026.149578: Cobalt-based thin films can mediate reversible sulfide uptake and anodic oxidation, but the underlying phase transformations have remained unresolved. Here, we investigate the mechanism of sulfide-driven charging and oxidative discharging of cobalt (oxy)hydroxide and oxide film anodes in alkaline electrolyte. Cyclic voltammetry, open-circuit potentiometry, and scan-rate-dependent linear sweep voltammetry show that sulfide first reduces CoOOH and Co₃O₄ to Co(OH)₂ before cobalt sulfide is formed. A thermodynamic analysis based on solubility-controlled formal potentials excludes direct CoS oxidation at the potential of the Co(OH)₂/Co₃O₄ transition. Instead, oxidation proceeds via an initial partial oxidation of lattice sulfide at relatively negative potentials, followed by the formation of Co(OH)₂ and its anodic conversion to Co₃O₄, which promotes further sulfide oxidation in an EC′-type process. At low scan rates, sulfide oxidation occurs predominantly in the Co(OH)₂/Co₃O₄ redox domain, demonstrating strong kinetic control of the solid-state conversion. The same kinetic effects further reveal that the initial oxidation of Co(OH)₂ proceeds via Co₃O₄ as an intermediate rather than directly to CoOOH. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for cobalt-mediated sulfide storage and oxidation and help explain the distinctive behaviour of cobalt-containing sulfide anodes in bioelectrochemical systems.
10.1016_j.ijheatmasstransfer.2026.128683: The battery market experienced an annual growth of 30 – 40% in recent years, particularly due to the increasing demand for electric vehicles. Nowadays, the most common type are lithium-ion batteries due to the high energy density and number of possible charge cycles. To maximize the service life of a lithium-ion battery pack it is essential that the operating temperature is kept between 15 – 35 °C. Therefore, a battery thermal management system is indispensable. The present work introduces an extended multiscale simulation approach that can be seen as an extension of the classical heat exchanger cell method . It enables detailed results for field variables of an entire battery pack at relatively low computational cost. Only information about the flow pattern inside the heat exchanger and the inlet temperature of the system is required, making the methodology applicable to complex or newly developed structured heat exchangers. The battery pack is divided into repetitive units (unit cells), which are simulated in detail by coupling computational fluid dynamics and a finite element method (CFD-FEM). The individual unit cells are then interconnected to yield the results for the entire battery pack. This approach overcomes the computational limitations associated with large and complex geometries. The presented methodology is applied to a 18650 battery pack consisting of 448 individual battery cells and a cooling plate with sinusoidally structured cooling channels under different load and operating conditions. The present work demonstrates that the extended multiscale integration approach can be used flexibly to evaluate the cooling performance of a battery pack under different conditions, providing valuable information for the design and analysis of cooling plates. For validation, a full-scale simulation of the battery pack was conducted. As the total cooling heat flow and the total pressure drop resulting from the large-scale integration model only deviated from the full-scale simulation by 2.84% and 1.17%, respectively, it can be concluded that this extended multiscale simulation approach presents a good compromise between computational effort and model accuracy.
10.1021_acsami.5c22446: Designing a highly robust oxygen evolution reaction (OER) electrocatalyst under industrially relevant conditions, especially repeated start-up and shutdown cycling, is crucial to achieving efficient electrolysis when connected to a renewable energy source, such as wind and solar, for mass hydrogen production. This study investigates the degradation mechanisms of finely synthesized NiFe-, CoFe-, and CoNiFe-LDH via operando Raman and operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy and electrochemical analysis. The most active NiFe-LDH degraded severely under repeated on–off cycles versus constant OER operation due to a decrease in the conductivity of the catalyst, suppression of Ni oxidation, and amorphization. CoFe-LDH had the most degraded OER performance among the investigated catalysts under intermittent operation due to the large structural changes and significant Fe dissolution during cycling. In contrast, CoNiFe-LDH exhibited exceptional durability because of its high structural stability and redox robustness arising from its intermediate structural framework and modified electronic interaction with the coexistence of Co and Ni. Co helped Ni to oxidize more easily and contributed to maintaining its redox ability. The CoNiFe-LDH demonstrated noteworthy on–off durability under industrially relevant conditions (600 mA cm –2, 60 °C), indicating that CoNiFe-LDH is a promising OER electrocatalyst for durable alkaline electrolyzers.
10.1029_2025wr040350: The presence of a reservoir along a river modifies downstream flood events by storing and releasing water volumes. By attenuating the peak flows, the structure significantly alters their corresponding probability distributions, particularly in terms of the shape of the distribution. These shape changes result primarily from the reservoir capacity to variably attenuate flood peaks associated with different return periods, where the effect can range from maximum attenuation to acting as a transparent system. Since flood observations often provide limited insight into the reservoir effect, understanding the underlying physical processes is essential for accurate estimation of peak discharge distributions. Here, we propose an analytical approach to evaluate the modification of the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of flood peaks, both from natural conditions (ante‐operam) to post‐reservoir conditions (post‐operam) and vice versa. It can be applied both to reservoir design and to the assessment of reservoir impacts based on real discharge data. In particular, the framework incorporates key system parameters and processes, including the available reservoir volume, its area, the maximum discharge of an uncontrolled spillway and the statistical characteristics of the inflow hydrograph. Some simplifications are introduced to derive an analytical closed‐form solution such as assuming a triangular hydrograph shape. The potential of the method is successfully demonstrated through an illustrative example and a real case study, where it is shown how the framework effectively captures the tail behavior of the peak discharge distribution. Specifically, the proposed solution captures well the effect of large hydrological variability on peak discharge reduction.
